units.text: Among freshwater macroinvertebrates, Odonata (Insecta) are a good model taxon for exploring the effects of climate warming on freshwater biodiversity because (1) they originated in the tropics, which implies tolerance to high temperatures; (2) adults present high morphological differentiation across species, which facilitates capture, identification and recording; (3) they occur with medium to high local abundances and are present in almost all freshwater habitats, with high species turnover due to larval and adult preferences in habitat use and evident niche partition among species; (4) they present high phenotypic variability, both within and between species, in traits pre-sumably involved in adaptation to climate warming, such as emergence and duration of flight season; and (5) there is a large and wellknown body of historical research, including extensive recording and rich historical datasets from citizen science projects (Corser et al., 2014; Hassall & Thompson, 2008; Termaat et al., 2019).

F I G U R E 1 (a) Proposed categories of potential range shifts based on differences between current and future species distribution in terms of longitude and latitude; (b) species occurrence map covering the Iberian Peninsula and Northern Morocco from six datasets.

The study area covered the westernmost Mediterranean region with a total number of 84 species, 25 occurring exclusively in the Iberian Peninsula and 9 restricted to Morocco (Torralba-Burrial & Ocharan, 2013). Occurrence of adults was compiled from six datasets (Figure 1b, see details at ‘Data Availability Statement’): (1) Oxygastra, the Catalan Odonata Study Group; (2) ROLA’s project of the environmental education association ‘El Bosque Animado’; (3) the Arthropod Collection of the University of Oviedo (Torralba-Burrial & Ocharan, 2013); (4) the Valencian Natural History Museum; (5) the

Asociacion de Naturalistas del Sureste (ANSE); and (6) the Moroccan  dataset collected by Mohamed El Haissoufi. When combining datasets, only records with taxonomic identification at the species level and observations after 2003, when more data and precise spatial coordinates started to be recorded systematically, were considered. For modelling purposes, in order to homogenise the sample effort and to reduce the spatial autocorrelation associated with environmental variables (see below), the presences of a species in $a 1 - k m ^ { 2 }$ grid cell were brought together and defined as a single detection, whereas the nooccurrence of a species at a given $1 { \cdot } { \mathsf { k m } } ^ { 2 }$ cell over several years of sampling was considered as a true absence (Supporting information S1). The data used are currently the main contribution of the Iberian data at [gbif.org](http://gbif.org) and at the Atlas of the European dragonflies and damselflies (Boudot & Kalkman, 2015). However, we avoided using data records directly from GBIF because they were collected following different protocols in each region and also including ‘opportunistic’ species without a harmonised sampling effort or geographical representativeness.

In order to assess how individual species potential distributions could change in the future based on current occurrences and using climatic conditions as predictors, species distribution models (SDMs) were used. SDM methods have been widely debated because future predictions are frequently over-interpreted (Araújo & Peterson, 2012), especially when limited occurrence data in high-dimensional environmental space are used (Peterson, 2011). While acknowledging this criticism, our intent was not to accurately map the future ranges of species, but to evaluate the models and classify the species into the five proposed range-shift categories. Since model performance decreases with sample size (Stockwell & Peterson, 2002), 10 species were discarded because they had been recorded in less than 20 localities (Supporting information S1).

To remove the redundant information of bioclimatic variables, Spearman correlation and variance inflation factor (VIF) analyses were performed with all bioclimatic values extracted from all occurrence points. To purge highly correlated bioclimatic variables, the biological and ecological meaning of each variable was considered. Finally, the

To determine the current species distribution, binary logistic generalised linear models (GLM) and boosted regression trees (BRT) were run for each species because testing for several algorithms is suggested to optimise the predictions for each particular species (Konowalik & Nosol, 2021; Qiao et al., 2015). GLM represents a flexible extension of linear models that allows for response variables that have a non-normal distribution error (binomial in the case of binary responses), whereas BRT combines regression trees for generating large numbers of simple distribution models that are selected for the best prediction by boosting algorithms (Elith et al., 2008; Franklin, 2010; Kienast et al., 2012). To create the input SDM matrix, the current bioclimatic information was extracted for each spatial point. The database created for each species was split into 70% as training set and 30% as testing set by random partition to validate the models. Each model was evaluated independently by three predictors of significance to select the model with the best performance: (1) by means of area under curve (AUC) statistics from a receiver-operating characteristic analysis (ROC), which is a threshold-independent evaluation of model discrimination (Fielding & Bell, 1997); (2) by true skills statistics (TSS), which is a measure of accuracy (Allouche et al., 2006) and (3) by odds ratio skill score (ORSS), which measures skill compared to a random prediction (Stephenson, 2000). AUC and TSS were the two metrics that achieved the highest performance compared to other evaluation models (Konowalik & Nosol, 2021) (Supporting information S2). The widely used logistic regression (fitted with GLM) was selected for the majority of species. However, for some species that had low numbers of occurrences (fewer than 70 grid cells), the BRT models (learning $\mathsf { r a t e } = 0 . 0 0 1$ , bag fraction = 0.75) performed better than GLM, as previously suggested (Konowalik & Nosol, 2021). All models were performed and evaluated using the R software (R Core Team, 2016) and the package ‘gbm (Ridgeway et al., 2015).

The first fPCA axis of the functional space (Figure 4a; Supporting information S8) explained 20.85% of the total variability, whereas the second and third axes explained respectively 13.62% and 10.94%. The trait categories most correlated to the first axis were semivoltinism (NC0) together with the opposite patterns of behaviour fliers (FBF) versus perchers (FBP), and the water quality oligotrophic (WO) versus eutrophic (WE). The second axis was mostly related with the opposite directions of absence (DN) versus presence (DY) of egg diapause. The trait categories most correlated with axes (>0.6) were selected (Supporting information S9).
